query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A hybrid machine-learning workflow that uses actively learned ML interatomic potentials trained on ab initio data from both solid and liquid phases near the fusion point, combined with a perturbative reweighting scheme to restore ab initio free-energy fidelity, can substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties relative to explicit ab initio MD and TOR-TILD.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental, binary, and multicomponent high-entropy alloys at high-temperature conditions near the melting point, where both solid and fluid phases have complex free-energy landscapes with significant contributions from vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
generation.intervention: Develop and implement an ML-driven potential framework that is actively trained on strategically sampled ab initio configurations from both phases; then, perform low-cost molecular dynamics using the ML potential with a targeted perturbative or reweighting correction applied to the free energies.
generation.conditions: Simulations performed near the melting temperature for systems ranging from single elements to up to 5–6 principal component high-entropy alloys; the training data must span both ordered (solid) and disordered (liquid) regimes to capture all relevant entropy contributions and anharmonic effects.
generation.structural_mediator: The interatomic potential landscape described by the ML model, which is augmented by ab initio corrections (via reweighting) to enforce proper vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration coupling physics.
generation.mechanism: The ML potential efficiently approximates the energy landscape across both phases at a fraction of the cost of full ab initio MD, while the reweighting scheme corrects any residual discrepancies. This dual strategy preserves the detailed entropy contributions from vibrations and anharmonic motions, ensuring free energy differences remain faithful to ab initio values.
generation.predicted_outcome: The hybrid ML–ab initio approach is expected to compute phase free energies and derived observables (e.g., melting curves, latent heats) with accuracies within a few meV/atom relative to explicit ab initio MD, but at 3–10 times faster computational speed and with improved scalability for multicomponent systems compared to TOR-TILD.
generation.baseline: Explicit ab initio molecular dynamics evaluations and the TOR-TILD method, which, while accurate in simpler systems, are either computationally prohibitive or slow for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
generation.boundary: Composition boundaries extend from elemental systems through binary alloys to multicomponent high-entropy alloys (up to 5–6 principal elements); temperature conditions are limited to the high-temperature regime near and above the fusion point where anharmonic and vibrational entropy contributions are critical.
generation.uncertainty: The exact speedup factor and fidelity level (in terms of meV/atom accuracy) may vary depending on the quality and representativeness of the ab initio training set and the efficiency of the reweighting scheme; further empirical calibration and testing are required to precisely quantify these gains.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a set of free-energy calculations for a chosen multicomponent high-entropy alloy near its melting point using (i) the hybrid ML–ab initio workflow and (ii) a full explicit ab initio MD simulation. Ensure that the training set for the ML model covers key configurations of both the solid and liquid phases. Apply the perturbative reweighting scheme to obtain ab initio-level free energies with the ML approach.
measurements: Phase free energy differences for both solid and liquid phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hybrid ML–ab initio method shows systematic deviations in free energy differences greater than ± a few meV/atom, or if the melting curve and latent heat predictions differ significantly (outside the anticipated error bounds) from those obtained by full ab initio MD and experimental benchmarks, then the hypothesis that the approach maintains ab initio level fidelity while offering computational speedup is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In recent years, many works have introduced computational methods to identify and characterize alloys with tailored properties, such as the solid solution strengthening, hardness, ductility index, and thermodynamic stability. Moreover, some of these methods have been employed in the context of the optimization of several target properties,, with the relevant material properties being obtained from various modeling approaches using experimental and theoretical input. For example, methods based on machine learning (ML) use various sets of descriptors partly derived from ab initio calculations in order to fit experimental data. This approach, however, often requires large data sets and, most crucially, it is intrinsically interpolative and cannot give predictions outside the domain covered by an existing data set. A more transferable methodology is to use properties of elements, or simple compounds, for extrapolation of target properties to multi-component properties, mainly using the rule-of-mixture. The search for distinct configurations is conducted using a progressively decreasing extrapolation grade, starting from 1000 and gradually reducing to 100, 10, and finally 2. We iterate multiple times, with always newly generated training candidate sets and stop when no new training configurations emerge anymore that exceeds the extrapolation grade. frame.system: High-temperature elemental, binary, and multicomponent high-entropy alloys undergoing melting (fusion) where both solid and liquid phases need faithful free-energy representations including vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
frame.goal: To obtain fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties (i.e. accurate free energies and derived observables) at a substantially reduced computational cost relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics and TOR-TILD, while preserving the fidelity of entropy contributions, anharmonic effects, and electron–vibration coupling.
frame.limitation: Traditional methods—explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation and TOR-TILD—are either computationally prohibitive (especially due to the cost of MD sampling for capturing anharmonicities and electron–vibration coupling) or scale poorly with increasing system complexity (e.g. multicomponent high-entropy alloys).
root_cause_cues: require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained
slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems
constraints: The free energies of both solid and fluid states must remain faithful
All relevant entropy terms (including vibrational contributions and effects from anharmonicities and electron–vibration coupling) must be retained in the model
frame.regime: High-temperature conditions near the fusion point for both solid and fluid states, with the composition range extending from elemental to binary, and ultimately multicomponent high-entropy systems.
prior_attempts: Explicit ab initio molecular dynamics: Highly accurate but prohibitively expensive for capturing complete free-energy landscapes with all entropy contributions.
TOR-TILD method: Successfully increased throughput for elemental and binary systems but suffers from substantial slowdowns when extended to complex, multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
frame.understanding: A methodological intervention is needed that streamlines the evaluation of free-energy differences between phases without sacrificing the detailed accuracy (vibrational, anharmonic, electron–vibration effects) provided by ab initio approaches.
frame.proposed_hypothesis: Integrate machine-learning (ML) interatomic potentials trained on strategically sampled ab initio data to serve as accurate surrogates for the energy landscape across both solid and liquid phases, and then apply perturbative or correction schemes (e.g., reweighting strategies) to recover ab initio fidelity in free energies. This hybrid ML–ab initio approach should capture key entropy contributions and anharmonic effects efficiently, drastically reducing the number of expensive MD simulations needed compared to traditional explicit ab initio MD and outperforming TOR-TILD in complex multicomponent systems.
frame.predicted_performance: The ML-driven workflow is expected to achieve free-energy evaluations 3–10 times faster than explicit ab initio MD while maintaining high fidelity (within a few meV/atom) over phase free energies, surpassing the efficiency of TOR-TILD especially for high-entropy systems.

boundaries.composition: From single-element systems through binary alloys to multicomponent high-entropy alloys (with a defined range of, for example, up to 5–6 principal elements).
boundaries.temperature: Focused on high-temperature regimes near and above the melting point, where anharmonic and vibrational entropy contributions are critical.

frame.supporting_evidence: Successful demonstrations of ML potential frameworks in capturing phase behavior and free energy surfaces in elemental and binary systems (as reported in earlier studies), which indicate that with a careful training set and correction methodology, similar accuracy can be extended to more complex systems.
frame.decisive_benchmark: Direct comparison of phase free energies and derived observables (such as melting curves and latent heats) from the ML–augmented workflow with those obtained from full ab initio MD simulations. Falsification would occur if the hybrid method systematically deviates beyond ± a few meV/atom in free-energy differences or incorrectly predicts phase boundaries relative to both experimental data and full ab initio benchmarks.

decision.trend: Early methods for obtaining fusion free energies relied on fully explicit ab initio molecular dynamics simulations, which—while highly accurate—proved prohibitively expensive especially when all relevant entropy contributions (vibrational, anharmonicity, electron–vibration coupling) were retained for both liquid and solid phases. An intermediate solution (TOR-TILD) improved throughput for simpler elemental and binary systems, but its performance degrades with multicomponent high-entropy materials. More recently, there has been a shift toward integrating data‐driven techniques: several works have successfully used machine-learning (ML) potentials and active learning to approximate energy landscapes with ab initio accuracy in screening and property trade‐off studies, as evidenced by frameworks that incorporate ab initio corrections into surrogates. However, these ML approaches have yet to be fully exploited for computing complete free-energy differences across phase transitions in complex alloys.
decision.unsolved: The key unsolved challenge is to faithfully capture the free energies for both solid and liquid phases, including all entropy contributions (vibrational, anharmonic, electron–vibration coupling), without incurring the extreme computational cost of full ab initio MD or the complexity scaling limitations of TOR-TILD in multicomponent systems.
decision.lever: Develop a hybrid ML workflow that trains interatomic potentials on strategically sampled ab initio data spanning both the solid and liquid regimes near the melting point, combined with a perturbative reweighting (or correction) scheme to restore ab initio fidelity in free-energy differences.
decision.why: This approach follows the observed trend of leveraging ML surrogates to accelerate high-fidelity simulations in elemental and binary systems while addressing the open question of scalable free-energy evaluation in multicomponent alloys. By focusing on strategic sampling and correction, the method is expected to reduce computational cost (achieving free-energy evaluations 3–10 times faster than explicit ab initio MD) and maintain accuracy to within a few meV/atom. The boundaries would encompass elemental to 5–6 component high-entropy alloys at temperatures near and above melting, building on supporting evidence from prior works that have demonstrated the effectiveness of ML-driven potentials in capturing phase behavior.
